TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the evolution of what used to be known as SSL.

It is used to protect HTTP traffic between a server and a browser: whatever crosses the public network travels encrypted.

To achieve this it relies on the building blocks from the previous lesson: symmetric and asymmetric keys, hash, and certificates.
TLS is the security layer that the HTTP of a secure site travels over.
Asymmetric to authenticate, symmetric for data

TLS uses both types of encryption, each where it performs best:

  • Asymmetric for authentication: a key pair and a certificate prove identity.
  • Symmetric for data exchange: it is far more efficient computationally.

The complication with symmetric encryption was distributing the key. The handshake solves that: both ends agree on how to exchange the symmetric keys before sending any data.
Asymmetric at the start, to know who I'm talking to; symmetric afterward, to talk fast.

The handshake is the way a client connects to a server protected by TLS.

The first three messages, SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK, are not TLS: they are part of TCP. TLS first needs an established connection to work on.

So far nothing is encrypted yet.
Client Hello: here's what I support

With the connection established, the client sends a Client Hello: it indicates that it requests a secure connection and sends the list of cipher suites it supports.

The list is ordered by preference. The server will choose the highest one it can support.
The client proposes; the server decides.

A cipher suite groups the cryptographic algorithms of the connection. For each one we know:

  • Key exchange: how the symmetric keys will be exchanged.
  • Authentication: how authentication will be done.
  • Bulk encryption: the symmetric key algorithm to use.
  • MAC (Message Authentication Code): the method for checking integrity.
The cipher suite name sums up the four algorithms the connection will use.
The client sends several, from most preferred to least preferred. The server goes down the list and keeps the highest one it can support; that is the one it reports in the Server Hello.
Client Hello list · order of preference

The server answers with the Server Hello, where it reports the selected cipher.

Along with it, it sends a Certificate: a document generated by a certificate authority, with which the server proves its identity.
Certificates and the chain of trust

The certificate has an issuer element: the one who issued it. That builds a chain of trust that ends at a ROOT CA, a company dedicated to generating certificates.

If the certificate was issued by a ROOT CA that I trust, I accept it as valid.

It may be issued by the ROOT CA or by an intermediate entity; that is why the server must send the whole chain, so the client can analyze it.
I trust the server because I trust whoever signed its certificate.
The client climbs up the issuer links until it reaches a root it already trusts.
Change Cipher Spec and encrypted data

The handshake ends with Change Cipher Spec: each side announces that it is switching to the agreed encryption.

From then on the application data (the HTTP) is sent, encrypted with the symmetric key algorithm of the chosen cipher suite.
Everything before was to get to this point: encrypted data between two ends that have already agreed.

In the handshake we saw, only the server presents a certificate. Client authentication (TLS mutual authentication) is optional.

After the Server Hello, the server can ask the client to present its certificate.

It is not widely used, because dealing with certificates is complex.

• TLS: evolution of SSL; protects HTTP between browser and server.
  • Asymmetric to authenticate, symmetric for the data.
  • Handshake: TCP → Client Hello (cipher suites) → Server Hello + Certificate → Change Cipher Spec → data.
  • Cipher suite: key exchange, authentication, symmetric encryption, and MAC.
  • The certificate is valid if its chain reaches a trusted ROOT CA.
